nameStory: White dittany gets its name from the ancient Greek city of Dicte on Crete, where a similar aromatic plant was first discovered. The 'white' refers to its pale, fragrant flowers that bloom in early summer. This plant has been prized since ancient times for its lemony fragrance and medicinal properties.
description: White dittany is a rare perennial herb that grows 2-4 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. It produces showy spikes of white or pale pink flowers with long, prominent stamens that give them a delicate, almost ethereal appearance. The compound leaves are dark green and release a strong citrusy scent when crushed. This member of the citrus family is extremely uncommon in New England, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White to pale pink flowers arranged in tall, terminal spikes with five petals and long, curved stamens that extend well beyond the petals, giving a wispy appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 9-11 oval leaflets that smell strongly of lemon when crushed or bruised, similar to citrus peel

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy perennial herb growing 2-4 feet tall with multiple sturdy stems arising from the base

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Star-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing small black seeds with a distinctive five-pointed appearance

habitat: White dittany is found in well-drained, alkaline soils in sunny to partially shaded locations, often in gardens or naturalized areas near old homesteads. In New England, it's most likely encountered as an escaped garden plant in areas with limestone-rich or amended soils. Look for it along old stone walls or in abandoned garden sites.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in late spring with fresh green compound leaves that are already fragrant when touched.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in early to mid-summer with showy white flower spikes lasting several weeks, followed by developing seed capsules.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to ground level with no above-ground parts visible until the following spring.

funFact: On hot, windless summer evenings, white dittany can actually be set on fire! The plant releases so much volatile citrus oil that you can light the vapors around the flowers with a match, earning it the nickname 'burning bush' - though the plant itself doesn't burn.
confusionNotes: The long, protruding stamens and strong citrus scent when leaves are crushed distinguish white dittany from other white-flowered perennials. The compound leaves and flower spike arrangement are quite distinctive once you know what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dittany,' this plant is completely different from the oregano-like dittany of Crete. White dittany is actually related to citrus trees, which explains its lemony fragrance. It's sometimes called 'gas plant' due to its flammable vapors.
compareHints: White dittany is the only Dictamnus species found in New England. Among other citrus family members in our region, it's unique for its herbaceous growth habit and compound leaves - most other Rutaceae here are woody plants like prickly ash or planted citrus relatives that don't survive our winters.
